content: Why is the Two Pointers technique on a sorted array more efficient than checking every pair?
expectedEvidence: Because the sorted property allows us to definitively eliminate a pointer at each step, reducing O(N^2) to O(N).

content: In Two Sum II, if the sum of elements at left and right pointers is too large, what must you do and why?
expectedEvidence: Decrement the right pointer to try a smaller sum, since the array is sorted.

content: Implement Two Sum II returning the 1-indexed positions of the two numbers.
expectedEvidence: While left < right, check sum. If sum < target left++, if sum > target right--, else return indices.

content: Why is your loop condition left < right and not left <= right for finding two distinct elements?
expectedEvidence: Because we need two distinct elements, so left cannot equal right.

content: Explain why this algorithm guarantees finding the pair if it exists, without skipping over it.
expectedEvidence: By moving only the pointer that must be moved to approach the target, we never skip the valid pair.

content: Give an example of an array where moving both pointers at once when sum != target would fail.
expectedEvidence: Target 5. Array: [1, 2, 4, 6]. Left=0, Right=3. Sum=7. Moving both gives Left=1, Right=2 (Sum=6). We missed [1,4].

content: Can Two Sum II be further optimized in time complexity below O(N)?
expectedEvidence: No, because we might need to examine every element at least once.

content: How would you use two pointers to square elements of a sorted array (which may contain negative numbers) and return a new sorted array?
expectedEvidence: Pointers at both ends (most negative and most positive), compare squares, place largest at the end of new array.
